result.topic_en: Euler gives a final numerical example (4n−1=103). He observes that every prime factor of the numbers n+q²+q is a quadratic residue of the prime 4n−1, and that this can fail when 4n−1 is composite (n=30, 4n−1=119). He then states this as a conclusion and proves a general theorem that a is a residue of the prime 4as±T, where T=(2q+1)²−4at.
result.transcription:
14°. Sit $4n-1=103$; $n=26$.
$p = 2.13, 2^2.7, 2^5, 2.19, 2.23, 2^3.7, 2^2.17, 2.41,$
$2.7^2, 2^2.29$, etc.
$r = 1, 2, 7, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 41$, etc.

Scholion.

§. 20. Ex his exemplis iterum abunde patet, omnes plane numeros primos in numeris $p$ contentos ipsos quoque esse residua. Euidens autem est, vt primum hoc de minoribus numeris fuerit certum, de maioribus nullum amplius dubium relinqui; at vero in numeros $p$ binarius non ingreditur, nisi iam fuerit in ipso numero primo $n$; ternarius autem, nisi in duobus primis insit, ex tota serie $p$ excluditur. Eodem modo patet, quinarium, nisi in tribus primis insit, quoque excludi; septenarius autem penitus excluditur, nisi in quatuor primis iam occurrat, et sic de reliquis. Vnde patet, in continuatione vlteriori istius seriei nullos numeros primos minores ingredi posse, qui non iam ante fuerint ingressi; quae obseruatio fortasse ad demonstrationem deducere posset. Verum hic iterum probe notetur, hanc insignem proprietatem tantum locum habere, quoties $4n-1$ fuerit numerus primus; si enim esset compositus, tum vtique eiusmodi numeri primi occurrere possunt, de quibus neutiquam liquet, vtrum in ordinem $r$ sint referendi. Veluti si fuerit $n=30=2.3.5$; tum numeri pro $p$ ita se habebunt:
$p = 2.3.5, 2^5, 2^2.3^2, 2.3.7, 2.5^2, 2^2.3.5, 2^3.3^2,$
$2.43, 2.3.17, 2^3.3.5[?], 2^2.5.7, 2.9^2$, etc.
Hic

Hic quidem statim adparet, binarium ad residua esse referendum; quo sublato iudicium redit ad sequentes numeros:
$3.5, 3^2, 3.7, 5^2, 43, 3.17, 5.7, 3^4$, etc.
Hinc autem nullo modo concludi potest, siue 3, siue 5, siue 7 in residuis reperiri; et fieri posset, vt singuli essent non-residua; quandoquidem producta ex binis non-residuis producunt residua; verum etiam hinc numerus $4n-1=119$ non est primus. De primis autem certa videtur haec

Conclusio.

§. 21. Quoties numerus $4n-1$ fuerit primus per eumque diuidantur omnia quadrata; non solum omnes numeri in forma $n+qq+q$ contenti inter residua occurrunt ipsi, sed etiam omnes plane factores primi, ex quibus illi sunt compositi.

Theorema generale.

§. 22. Denotante T numerum quemcunque in hac formula $(2q+1)^2-4at$ contentum, si fuerit vel $4as+T$, vel $4as-T$ numerus primus, per eumque quadrata diuidantur, tum in residuis semper reperietur numerus $a$.

Demonstratio.

Cum enim sit $T=(2q+1)^2-4at$; numerus ille primus erit vel $4as-4at+(2q+1)^2$, vel $4as+4at-(2q+1)^2$. Illo casu habebimus $p=a(s-t)$; hoc vero $p=a(s+t)$, sicque in vtroque casu $p$ factorem habet $a$, qui ergo per praecedentes conclusiones in residuis ex quadratis ortis occurret.

Euleri Opusc. Anal. Tom. I.      N n      Co-

items.quote: omnes plane numeros primos in numeris $p$ contentos ipsos quoque esse residua
items.english: All prime numbers contained in the numbers p are themselves also residues.

items.quote: Vnde patet, in continuatione vlteriori istius seriei nullos numeros primos minores ingredi posse, qui non iam ante fuerint ingressi; quae obseruatio fortasse ad demonstrationem deducere posset.
items.english: Hence it is clear that, as the series is continued further, no smaller primes can enter that have not already entered; this observation might perhaps lead to a proof.

items.quote: Quoties numerus $4n-1$ fuerit primus per eumque diuidantur omnia quadrata; non solum omnes numeri in forma $n+qq+q$ contenti inter residua occurrunt ipsi, sed etiam omnes plane factores primi, ex quibus illi sunt compositi.
items.english: Whenever 4n−1 is prime and all squares are divided by it, not only do all numbers of the form n+q²+q occur among the residues, but so do all the prime factors of which they are composed.

items.quote: Denotante T numerum quemcunque in hac formula $(2q+1)^2-4at$ contentum, si fuerit vel $4as+T$, vel $4as-T$ numerus primus, per eumque quadrata diuidantur, tum in residuis semper reperietur numerus $a$.
items.english: Let T denote any number of the form (2q+1)²−4at. If either 4as+T or 4as−T is a prime number and squares are divided by it, then the number a will always be found among the residues.
